audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated locators in the held Lobel 2013, Kaufman & Himmelmann and Lobel 2005 files. (2) But the deciding evidence is second-hand and indirect: a footnote about Maranao citing an unpublished 2003 talk, a survey paraphrase of that footnote, accent marks in an angry-register paper, and unsourced Wikipedia; the record's own caution flag says so. (3) McFarland 1974, the standard first-hand dialect survey (author resident in Iriga), was downloaded now from the Internet Archive copy of Zorc's site and read: Table 1 p.30 and p.31 state that vowel length is phonemically distinctive in Iriga (a: Iriga City) and Iriga (b: Baao/Bato/Nabua) as in all Bikol dialects, that stress/loudness is not distinctive, that length is confined to non-final vowels before a single consonant, and p.41 that penult length is 'fixed arbitrarily in the lexicon'; p.51 add

sources.quote: p.30 Table 1 'Phonemic inventories of the Bikol area dialects': row 'Vowel length' marked X for Inventory B (Daraga, Oas, Iriga City = Iri(a)) and for Iri(b) (Baao, Bato, Nabua). p.31: 'Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not. Distinctive vowel length may occur between any vowel other than the final vowel of a word and a single consonant; e.g. Leg sa:lug 'river' (cf. salug 'floor') ... Length is non-distinctive after the final vowel of a word. In inherited words, length does not occur before a consonant cluster.' p.41: 'Basic vowel length within
sources.note: The only first-hand phonological description covering Iriga/Rinconada (Glottolog's sole descriptive ref); states directly that vowel length is lexically distinctive in Iriga (both subdialects) and stress is not - replaces a second-hand footnote + Wikipedia as the deciding source.

tone.quote: In some cases, closely related Philippine languages appear to differ in whether they have phonemic length/stress contrasts. As Lobel (2013:287) notes, Maranao does not appear to have stress contrasts but its sister language, Maguindanao does (Sullivan 1986:11). Lobel further notes the loss of phonemic stress/length in Rinconada Bikol while Zorc (1978) and Himes (1998) discuss the same phenomenon in the South Cordilleran of Philippine languages.
